title: Conflict Resolution
summary: Resolving concurrent writes with last-write-wins, vector clocks, CRDTs, or application-level merges.

slides.markdown:
The moment you allow more than one node to accept a write to the same record — [multi-leader or leaderless replication](replication-strategies) — you've signed up for conflicts: two writes, no inherent order between them, both claiming to be correct.

This topic covers the actual toolbox for resolving that: the cheap-but-lossy default (last-write-wins), the detection mechanism that doesn't rely on clocks (vector clocks), and two ways to avoid picking a winner at all (CRDTs and application-level merges).

slides.sectionTitle: Why conflicts are inevitable once you allow concurrent writes
slides.markdown:
A **conflict** happens when two writes to the same piece of data occur without either one being aware of the other — neither happened "after" the other in any meaningful sense, they were simply concurrent. Once more than one node can accept writes independently (multi-leader, leaderless), there's no shared reference point that could have prevented this.

This isn't a bug to be engineered away — it's the direct, unavoidable consequence of the availability you bought by allowing multiple write points. The only real choice is *how* you resolve it: automatically with a rule, or explicitly with application logic.

Systems that claim "no conflicts" under multi-leader or leaderless replication are usually hiding a silent last-write-wins underneath.

slides.sectionTitle: Last-write-wins: simple, and what it silently throws away
slides.markdown:
**Last-write-wins (LWW)** resolves a conflict by attaching a timestamp to each write and keeping whichever has the later one, discarding the other entirely. It's simple to implement and requires no coordination — which is exactly why so many systems default to it.

The silent cost: the discarded write isn't merged, flagged, or recoverable — it's gone, with no signal to either the system or the user that anything was lost. Worse, if clocks across nodes aren't perfectly synchronized (they never are), "later" can be wrong — a write that happened first by wall-clock time can lose to one that happened second, purely because its node's clock was ahead.

LWW is a reasonable default only when losing a concurrent update is genuinely cheap — a cache entry, a "last seen" timestamp — never for data a user would notice vanishing.

slides.sectionTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrent writes without wall-clock time
slides.markdown:
A **vector clock** sidesteps the wall-clock problem entirely: instead of a timestamp, each write carries a small counter per replica — `{A:2, B:1}` means "this write reflects 2 operations this replica has seen from A and 1 from B." Comparing two vector clocks tells you their actual relationship: one **strictly dominates** the other (every count is >=, at least one is >) meaning it happened after, or **neither dominates** the other, meaning they were genuinely concurrent.

This is strictly more information than a timestamp gives you — instead of guessing at "later," the system can say with certainty "these two writes were concurrent and need resolving" versus "this one definitely came after that one, keep it."

The cost: every value now needs to track and compare vector clocks, and the system (or the application) has to decide what to do when it detects a genuine tie, rather than mechanically picking a winner.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: two concurrent writes and a vector clock detecting the conflict
slides.markdown:
![Vector clocks: a genuine conflict where neither dominates, vs a clear happened-before pair](assets/vector-clock-conflict.svg)

Comparing `{A:1, B:0}` against `{A:0, B:1}` shows neither one contains the other — that's the signature of a genuine conflict, not just a race in arrival time. Compare that to `{A:2, B:1}` against `{A:1, B:0}`, where every count in the second is less than or equal to the first — a clear "happened before" relationship, no conflict to resolve.

slides.sectionTitle: CRDTs: data types that merge without conflict by construction
slides.markdown:
A **CRDT** (conflict-free replicated data type) is a data structure designed so that merging any two divergent copies always produces the same result, regardless of the order operations arrived in — there's no "winner" to pick because the merge rule is mathematically guaranteed to converge.

A simple example: a counter that only ever increments, replicated across nodes, where merging means summing each replica's local count. There's no conflict because every operation composes cleanly with every other, by the type's design rather than by a runtime decision.

This pushes the resolution logic out of the application and into the data structure itself — you don't write conflict-handling code, you pick a CRDT whose merge semantics already match what you need. The next topic in this group goes deeper into the actual CRDT catalog.

slides.sectionTitle: Application-level merge (like a shopping cart union)
slides.markdown:
Sometimes the right merge rule isn't generic enough for a CRDT or a database default — it's specific to what the data *means*. **Application-level merging** hands the conflict to business logic that understands the domain: two concurrent edits to a shopping cart don't need a winner, they need a **union** — if replica A added a book and replica B added a pen, the merged cart has both.

Amazon's original Dynamo paper used exactly this example: rather than losing one of the two additions (LWW) or requiring a generic data type (a CRDT), the shopping-cart service merges by unioning item sets, occasionally re-adding an item a user had already removed — an acceptable trade-off since losing an added item is worse than briefly resurrecting a removed one.

This is the most flexible option and the most work: someone has to write and maintain that merge logic per data type.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: LWW vs vector clocks vs CRDTs on correctness and complexity
slides.markdown:
| | Last-write-wins | Vector clocks | CRDTs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Detects genuine concurrency | No — always picks a winner | Yes — explicitly flags concurrent writes | N/A — designed to merge without needing to detect a "winner" |
| Data loss risk | High — silently drops the loser | Low — surfaces the conflict for resolution | None, by construction, within the CRDT's semantics |
| Implementation complexity | Lowest | Moderate — track and compare clocks | Moderate to high — requires the right CRDT for the data shape |
| Who resolves the conflict | The clock, automatically | The application, when notified | The data type's merge function |

**How to decide:** LWW only where losing an update is cheap; vector clocks when you need to *know* a conflict happened and resolve it deliberately; CRDTs when the data naturally fits a mergeable shape (counters, sets) and you want conflict handling built in, not bolted on.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: last-write-wins silently dropping a concurrent update
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our database resolves write conflicts automatically, so we don't need to think about it."

**Why it's wrong:** "resolves automatically" almost always means last-write-wins under the hood, which doesn't reconcile the two writes — it deletes one of them, permanently, with no log entry a user or engineer can inspect later. Two support agents editing the same ticket, or two devices syncing the same note offline, can each believe their edit saved, while one silently vanished.

**Correct model:** before shipping a feature on multi-leader or leaderless replication, ask explicitly what should happen when two writes to the same record are concurrent. If the honest answer is "whichever's data loss is fine," LWW is acceptable. If it's not, reach for vector clocks, a CRDT, or an application-level merge — don't let the default silently make that call for you.
